title: To Give or Not to Give: The Talk as a Racial Socialization Practice
journal: Journal of Developmental and Life-Course Criminology
abstract: The Talk is commonly understood as a protective racial socialization strategy through which Black parents prepare their children for encounters with police. Using a grounded theory approach, this study examines not only how parents deliver The Talk, but why some intentionally refrain from it. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 30 Black parents in Ferguson, Missouri, conducted during the 2014 protests following the death of Michael Brown, we explore parental decision-making in a context of heightened racial tension and collective activism. Guided by an ecological and developmental framework, we analyze how parents assess risk, emotional readiness, and protection when socializing their children around policing. Findings reveal that parents who engaged in The Talk emphasized compliance strategies, constitutional rights, and avoidance as protective mechanisms. In contrast, parents who did not provide The Talk described intentional restraint, prioritizing respect for authority and concerns about instilling fear. Racial socialization strategies varied across families, with gender emerging as a particularly salient factor, as sons received more frequent and distinct messages. Together, these findings challenge assumptions that the absence of The Talk reflects parental inaction, instead highlighting both the presence and absence of The Talk as strategic approaches to protecting Black youth. Implications extend to Black parenting practices, parenting programs, and clinical interventions
